extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and researchers interested in peer review and scholarly-publishing reform
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and commentary for assessing manuscripts about peer review systems and for evaluating peer review models (traditional and open/novel variants). Focuses on evidence, clarity, scope, historical accuracy, and practical implementation issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about study design and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: “I support David Moher’s suggestion to be transparent about the study’s design and methods. It appears to be a narrative review… This should be acknowledged as a limitation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether the paper is a narrative vs systematic review; disclose strengths and limitations and the potential for selection bias in references. Be explicit about methodology used to gather and select literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims with empirical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions such as “has there been any research on hybrid peer review models to back this up?” illustrate the need to back strong positive claims (e.g., that a hybrid model “is more efficient, democratic, and accountable”) with research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If empirical studies exist, cite them; otherwise hedge language (e.g., 'we predict' or 'we hypothesise') and label assertions as speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate use of technical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: use of ‘oligarchic’ vs a more appropriate term ‘oligopolistic’ when describing publisher market structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose discipline-appropriate vocabulary and correct economic/legal terminology to avoid misleading characterisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide references for broad, alarming statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement that there is a “substantial corpus of studies that critically examine the technical aspects of peer review which… should be extremely worrisome” needs supporting citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make sweeping evaluative claims without pointing to representative literature; add citations or soften claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attributing sole causation without nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique: attributing retractions or widespread failures solely to peer review is misleading — multiple actors (authors, editors, reviewers) contribute to failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing causes of integrity problems, recognise multi-causality and avoid implying single-cause explanations unless supported by evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define ambiguous or loaded terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Example critique: “What do you mean by ‘oligarchic research institutes’? When does a research institute become ‘oligarchic’?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear definitions or operational criteria for non-obvious terms used to characterise organisations or systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer real-world studies over (or alongside) models when claiming practical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern that a cited pre-print modeling study is used to support claims about referee incentives; asks whether 'real world' studies back this up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between modeling/theoretical results and empirical observations; cite both where possible and label modeling limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite the correct source for specific empirical findings
rubrics_metrics.description: E.g., “Journals with higher transparency ratings… were less likely to accept flawed papers and showed a higher impact as measured by Google Scholar’s h5-index” — which referenced paper reported this?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute specific empirical findings to the precise source and ensure in-text citations match the referenced claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise about what publishing referee reports achieves
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagreement with phrasing: “while assessments of articles can never be evidence-based without the publication of referee reports..” — reviewer suggests 'publicly verifiable' instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully state the benefits of publishing referee reports (e.g., transparency, verifiability, accountability) and avoid overstating causal effects like 'evidence-based' without clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss advantages and disadvantages of peer review by endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2.5.3 should elaborate: author-recommended reviewers may be more likely to recommend acceptance and can be open to gaming (fake reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List potential biases (author-suggested reviewer bias), abuse vectors (fake reviewers), and mitigation strategies (editor oversight, verification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiate claims about PRE (publish-review engines / preprint-related claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements like “PRE is much cheaper, legitimate, unbiased, faster, and more efficient…” require evidence or should be presented as opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Back general comparative claims about cost, speed, bias, and legitimacy with data or tone them as conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain process differences when claiming faster publication
rubrics_metrics.description: “In theory, depending on the state of the manuscript, this means that submissions can be published much more rapidly, as relatively little processing is required” — reviewer asks why less processing is required in PRE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the specific steps reduced or eliminated in the alternative model and explain why this leads to measurable time savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary or unclear citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: “In any vision of the future of scholarly publishing (Kriegestorte et al., 2012)” — reviewer questions why a reference is needed there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each citation supports a claim; remove citations that do not substantively add evidence or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims about motivations to perform peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: “The most widely-held reason for performing peer review is a sense of academic altruism or duty…” — reviewer requests a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite surveys or studies of reviewer motivations or rephrase as anecdotal if no data available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent spelling and formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Typos/formatting inconsistencies noted (e.g., 'skepticism' vs 'scepticism'; 'decoupled the quality assessment' should be 'decouple').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread for consistent British/American spelling choices, grammar, and phraseology; fix typographical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be clear about intended audience and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer found the article massive and unclear about intended audience; suggests the difficulty in imagining who the paper is for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State target readership early (policy-makers, researchers, editors, general scientific audience) and tailor depth/length accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve focus and readability; avoid burying important points
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments: lack of focus makes the paper hard to read and important points are often buried amid less important material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise material, shorten or relocate less essential sections (e.g., lengthy history), and signpost main arguments clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between major-impact innovations and small-scale experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation: clearly separate innovations that have already had a major impact (e.g., peer print servers) from experimental approaches with limited adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate space proportionally to impact and provide criteria for what counts as 'major impact' (adoption rates, citations, platform uptake).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate peer review from reader commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: “It should make a clear distinction between peer review (as academics understand it) and reader commentary: the former plays a vital role in scholarly publishing, the role of the latter has been marginal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define roles, functions, and typical outcomes of formal peer review vs post-publication reader comments; avoid conflating them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise peer review’s role in improving manuscript quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer notes the role of peer review not only as gate-keeper but in improving manuscript quality and mentions interactive review models where reviewers and authors collaborate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss mechanisms by which review improves quality (feedback loops, interactive review), and cite examples (e.g., interactive Frontiers model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss the role of technology platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: “The role of the technology platforms, already used by Open Access and classical publishers. Good and bad platforms can be vital enablers for/obstacles to innovative forms of peer review.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse how platform features (workflows, moderation tools, scalability) enable or hinder review innovations; include examples of established vs experimental platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify how community-led governance should be formed and run
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions about whether community-run systems should be based on disciplinary societies, research labs, or something else and how they would be formed and governed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose concrete governance models, membership rules, nomination/election processes, and accountability mechanisms for community-run editorial systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify the future role and responsibilities of editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer asks whether editors would be democratically nominated moderators, whether they’d invite reviewers, and how they would prevent reviewer-selection skew.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe editorial responsibilities in proposed models (moderation, reviewer recruitment, conflict resolution), and explain workflows for accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address reviewer selection bias and workload distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Concern that if reviewers are free to choose papers, they may concentrate on fashionable topics or influential authors, leading to uneven reviewing loads and coverage gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss mechanisms to ensure equitable reviewer distribution (assignment algorithms, incentives, quotas) and mitigate popularity bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine incentives for referees
rubrics_metrics.description: “The present lack of bona fide incentives for referees is perhaps the main factor responsible for indifference to editorial outcomes…” — raises need to consider incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse incentive structures (credit, recognition, monetary or career incentives) and how they influence reviewer engagement and review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reviewer training and practical templates
rubrics_metrics.description: Author notes interest in training scholars, especially junior ones, and mentions a drafted peer review template to support first-time reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include or reference concrete training materials, checklists, and templated review forms to improve reviewer consistency and skill development.
